profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the bandit-evaluation research workstream and the ML platform workstream at a company preparing an internal review of a multi-armed bandit system for automated model deployment. The team has already run core experiments, and this meeting is to align on the interface between the research evaluation package and the ML Ops replay/deployment infrastructure before a Thursday handoff and a demo the following week. The agenda is to confirm which traces and event logs will be used, what the baseline comparison refers to in the shared report, what 'shadow evaluation' will look like for the next run, and what each side considers sufficient for the Thursday handoff. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on responsibilities, artifacts, and timing for the next evaluation cycle.

members.name: Dr. Priya Nandakumar
members.expertise: offline policy evaluation, contextual bandits, experiment analysis, reproducibility
members.background: Priya leads the research side of the project and has spent the last month comparing six model-selection strategies using replay over logged deployment traces; she previously worked in academic RL research and is comfortable handing off notebooks, config files, and result bundles to partner teams.
members.private_state: She wants the platform team to run one more validation pass using their infrastructure without forcing her group to package the work as a production-grade service yet, because her paper draft and appendix tables are due soon and she is trying to preserve the exact settings that produced the current results.
hidden_assumptions: When platform colleagues say 'shadow evaluation,' they usually mean offline replay against historical request logs rather than a live mirrored deployment.
If everyone says 'baseline,' they are referring to the latest research baseline documented in the shared experiment folder unless someone explicitly names a production router.
A handoff is 'ready' once the policy outputs, config, and replay instructions are reproducible by another technical team, even if nothing is containerized or monitored.
The relevant rollback data are the explicit rollback-trigger events emitted by the deployment controller table, not every model switch recorded elsewhere.

members.name: Ethan Morales
members.role: Senior ML Platform Engineer, Deployment Optimization
members.expertise: model serving, deployment telemetry, traffic mirroring, experiment plumbing
members.background: Ethan owns the evaluation pathway that connects candidate routing policies to deployment telemetry and has been preparing a mirrored-traffic setup so the bandit policy can be assessed in an ML Ops environment without serving user-facing responses.
members.private_state: He wants the research team to give him something that can slot into the existing deployment evaluation harness with minimal custom work, because his team is already supporting another launch and he assumes the research side is nearly ready for integration.
hidden_assumptions: In deployment discussions, 'shadow evaluation' means the policy runs on live mirrored traffic in the serving stack, even if its decisions are not exposed to users.
The default 'baseline' is the currently deployed routing logic behind the baseline-router feature flag, because that is what platform dashboards and comparisons use.
Something is only 'ready for handoff' if it conforms to the serving interface, has schema validation, and can be scheduled in the evaluation harness.

Rollback logs should include any event that reversed or interrupted a model promotion, including manual operator reversions and canary aborts, because those are all operationally meaningful rollbacks.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the next step is to run the policy in 'shadow evaluation.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means an offline replay pass over historical deployment traces using logged contexts and delayed outcomes, with no live system involvement.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a live shadow deployment receiving mirrored real-time requests in the serving stack, with predictions logged but not acted on.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both meanings are standard in adjacent ML workflows, and the phrase sounds precise enough that neither expects ambiguity; because both are non-user-facing evaluations, surface agreement feels complete.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the bandit results should be compared against 'the current baseline.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the epsilon-greedy heuristic from experiment bundle v17 that produced the comparison tables in the draft.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the production routing logic currently running behind the feature flag baseline-router in the deployment platform.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both objects are genuinely current baselines within their own workstreams, and each assumes the other is naturally anchoring to the most obvious one in a coordination meeting.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the package should be 'ready for handoff by Thursday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes readiness means a reproducible result bundle: policy score files, a config YAML, a README, and the exact replay command used for the appendix.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes readiness means an integration-ready artifact: a container or callable service endpoint, schema-checked inputs/outputs, and registration in the evaluation harness.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In coordination meetings, 'ready' is a common status shorthand, and both sides assume the surrounding workflow makes the completion criteria self-evident.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to include 'rollback logs' in the next evaluation pass.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes only explicit automated rollback-trigger events from the deployment controller, because those correspond to the failure signal studied in the paper.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes all reversal-like operational events, such as manual operator rollbacks, canary aborts, and model-switch cancellations from orchestration logs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about a familiar artifact category rather than a specific table definition, and the broader category seems harmlessly inclusive during a fast alignment conversation.

When I say shadow evaluation, I mean replay over the historical deployment traces with the same contexts, rewards, and controller events we've already been using.
